Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Vignette:
Samir stood in the doorway of the rented duplex on Elm Street, the way the floorboards groaned beneath his boots pulling him back to the autumn months when his marriage had fractured into violence. He had come to believe that the betrayal was absolute; the man he had shared his home, his finances, and his quiet routines with had become a source of sudden, physical force. Shoves against his chest, a heavy glass vase catching his shoulder, fists that found their mark without warning. Now, years later, the memories of that duplex did not arrive as a single story. They came in fragmented pieces—a sudden flash of the cracked sidelight, a disconnected image of a raised hand, the cold draft from the back door—all of them unspooling in his mind without sequence. What frightened him most was how his surroundings could instantly bring back the full memory without warning. A passing helicopter’s thrum from the nearby flight path would slice through the community center where he organized neighborhood assemblies, and instantly Samir was back in the living room, the sound wrapping around him like a physical presence. When those aircraft noises echoed over the city, Samir felt a familiar pressure in his ears, and sometimes he heard the sharp exhale of his partner’s voice, the specific creak of the floorboard where the impact landed. Those auditory echoes lived inside him long after the event. He had learned to brace himself against the geography of his daily life. The duplex itself, just a few blocks away, remained a spatial trap; he walked past it on his way to the transit hub but never turned down the side street, his pace quickening as if distance alone could keep the old violence at bay. Darker environments tightened their grip on him. He avoided the unlit storage room beneath the community center, the way the shadows pooled around the worktables, and the narrow alleys behind the apartment buildings that felt less like passages and more like enclosed spaces. When the light failed or the walls closed in, his body registered the impact zones. Samir’s work as a community organizer required him to move through clusters of people, but navigating a room now meant constant, quiet calculation. He watched faces and shoulders, vigilant for the subtle shifts that signaled dangerous people. A raised voice, a sudden step forward, a crowded doorway—each moment demanded his attention. He wore his clothing like armor, favoring thick cotton shirts, long sleeves, and high collars that kept his skin covered. The layers were not merely practical; they were a way to stay concealed, to avoid being noticed, to make himself a quiet presence among the crowds he organized. Over the months, these habits had accumulated. He missed informal gatherings because he preferred the periphery to the center. He scheduled his meetings during daylight hours and in rooms with wide windows. The work did not stop, but his position within it had narrowed. What sustained his quiet endurance were his interpretations, which coexisted with his sensory habits. He was certain that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he is; he had always been steady, predictable, the kind of man who absorbed pressure without flinching, and his own nature had made him the target. His broader beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed. He no longer trusted that safety was a permanent state, only a temporary condition that could be overturned. At fifty-four, Samir sat across from a therapist now, his hands resting on his knees, his sleeves buttoned to the wrist. He had finally made the appointment after a council meeting where the sudden drop of ambient light in the hall had frozen him mid-sentence, the aircraft hum above the roof sending the familiar images rushing back. He was not sure what recovery looked like to him, only that he was tired of bracing against the unseen. He hoped, perhaps, to walk past the duplex on Elm Street and simply keep walking.
